title: The crawl loop, and the filter that stops it running forever

spec.title: The crawl loop, and the filter that stops it running forever
spec.description: A crawler is a cycle: fetch, parse, discover new links, feed them back. The interesting parts are what keeps that cycle polite and what keeps it from revisiting the same pages endlessly.

steps.text: The crawl starts from a seed set — a hand-curated list of high-quality entry points. Everything the crawler ever reaches is discovered by following links out from these, so seed choice shapes coverage.

A fetcher takes the next URL. The frontier is not one queue — it is a queue per host, so that politeness can be enforced by rate-limiting each host independently while the crawler as a whole stays busy.
The page is fetched, subject to robots.txt and a per-host delay, and handed to the parser.
Content is persisted with a checksum, so a page whose bytes have not changed since last crawl can be skipped cheaply next time.

Extracted links are checked against the seen-URL filter. A Bloom filter answers 'definitely new' or 'probably seen' in constant space — at web scale an exact set of visited URLs does not fit in memory.
Only genuinely new URLs go back to the frontier, and the cycle repeats. Without this filter the crawler revisits the same pages forever and never reaches new ones.
Crawler traps: calendars with infinite 'next month' links, or URLs with session IDs that make every request look like a new page. The filter never fires because the URLs really are new.
Defences are depth limits per host, URL normalisation that strips known-volatile query parameters, and content checksums that catch pages which differ in URL but not in substance.

And a per-host budget, so one pathological domain cannot consume the whole crawl. The Bloom filter's false positives cut the same way: a small fraction of genuinely new pages are skipped, which is an acceptable trade for the memory saved.
